text:
Where could the cave leading to Ganondorf be located?

Recently, I actually went wandering through Hyrule Castle. I tried to find any possible clues that could help point to where Ganondorf might be held. I thought of 3 places.

The main hall: This area is mysteriously blocked off in BOTW, even though it's a massive part of the castle. There's an obvious doorway leading to it, but boulders block it. Perhaps they open it in the sequel and discover a way down to his chamber.

The circular room where you fight Calamity Ganon: This one makes a bit more sense, since it's the furthest area beneath the castle. Though it doesn't seem like there would be any openings to reach him from there.

One of the passages at the bottom of the castle: This would be places like the prison, or where you unlock the hidden shrine. There could easily be some kind of hidden opening somewhere. There's a lot of stone walls, and rocks that could easily be moved to reveal a passageway. Where specifically though, I have no idea.

It's just something I've been thinking about a lot. His body was right under us the whole time and we had no clue.. until the BOTW2 trailer.

text:
My biggest gripe with BotW, and what challenge runs can fix it?

This is something I don't see come up a lot, but it's way too easy.

Now, yes, you will get hit, a lot. But when healing items are so incredibly commonplace, by the time you're off the Great Plateau you never need to worry about your health again. All it is is a mild annoyance of opening your menu.

Now, what is a good run to deal with this? So far the best I've found is "you can only eat at cooking pots, towns, goddess statues, mini games, or stables; but elixers you can drink wherever"- which is good in conjunction with a warpless run, but beyond that? It just isn't fun. Alternatively, you can treat food like recovery hearts and eschew cooking entirely, saying you have to eat it as soon as you pick it up, which is annoying.

The best balance I found so far is the "no-eating-except-" rule from earlier combined with a warpless run, with the leniency that if you pick food up, you can always choose to immediately eat it raw. This lends to the finding-recovery-hearts style gameplay but still doesn't feel ideal.

How would you do it?

text:
Replaying MM3D, the worst change is still clearly Zora Link swimming

On a whim, I elected to charge up my 3DS and bring it with me on a recent international trip, which turned out to be a damn good decision, as we got stuck for 5 days with nothing to do.

Started a new save in MM3D and, given that there's been years since my last playthrough, I've had a lot of distance to assuage some of my prickliness at the changes in the remake.

I really like the remake on my second playthrough. Almost all of the noticeable changes made by Grezzo make a lot of sense to me and don't offend me any longer. The one change that still stands out as really terrible, however, is how they changed Zora Link swimming. Making the "power" swim movement tied to the barrier use really sucks, since the movement in the original was super fun. Being able to zip around the sea and pop out like a dolphin was very cool in the N64 version.

Not sure what the cause of the change was, but it makes Zora Link and the Great Bay parts of the game less fun.

The best change outside of how time and saving works has to be moving Shiro from the Ikana Canyon road to the middle of the Pirate Fortress. That's a brilliant change that just makes sense.

All in all, Zora Link swimming mechanics being the worst change means the remake was exceptionally well-done and the QoL changes to passage of time and saving make the remake superior to the original.

Breath of the Wild's first puzzle solved

Only a couple players seem to have found this on tape, but on the western side of Mount Hylia there's a circle of stones. The people in this video tried the obvious thing and bombed it, but the circle didn't react.

That's because the circle is incomplete. Link needs to pick up the lone rock, place it in the gap, and bomb the center of the ring to reveal a hole (or just a Korok will pop out, I don't know exactly).

But beyond the neat puzzle itself, I think this has positive implications for Breath as a whole. Not only does the stone circle suggest that the world will be more than a better version of Far Cry, with puzzles and points of interest about, but it also shows a new kind of puzzle. It clearly relies on knowledge of Ocarina of Time—by release a 19-year-old game. Players who get the reference will be challenged by the slight subversion of the rule, while new players will have to learn the exception and the rule all at once.

Why the Green River Zoras appeared only in the downfall timeline theory.

In Oracle of Ages the green Zoras were referred to as the river Zoras, basically a different sub species of zora that inhabit fresh water lakes and rivers.

I came up with this theory on why the Green River Zoras only appeared in the downfall timeline, and why the Zoras in Ocarina of Time looked so different now.

When Ganondorf ruled Hyrule he changed the waters in Hyrule to be less salty, akin to removing the extra chlorine in the water, or removing its density at least compared to the regular water we see in Ocarina of Time when Link was a child. But it also lead to the Zora to slowly evolve to accommodate this water. The first few generations looked the same, so they took no interest in the water. But their biology was slowly changing in each generation to better reflect it, such as having more fishy features and such.

The reason why don't see the river Zora in the adult timeline is because of the great flood so the Zora couldn't change into the river Zora, but instead they changed into the Rito.

The reason why we don't see the river Zoras in the child timeline is because Link was sent back to his childhood, so Ganondorf couldn't tamper with the water so the Zora remained the same.

I don't understand why so many people believe that the goddess statue in the Forgotten Temple is the same one from Sky Keep. In short, after Link uses the Triforce to annihilate Demise, Sky Keep crashes into Faron Woods (a region in southeast Hyrule), whereas the Forgotten Temple rests in Tabantha Frontier (a region in northwest Hyrule). I shouldn't need to point out that these locations lie on opposite corners of the map... Additionally, it was established in Hyrule Historia that Rauru builds over the ruins of the Sealed Temple when he constructs the Temple of Time. Breath of the Wild takes place millenia after Ocarina of Time, but even in Ocarina of Time, the goddess statue had already faded into obscurity.

What makes much more sense to me would be if the goddess statue from the Isle of Songs became the same statue in the Forgotten Temple. Not only are both statues comparable in age and stature, but the Isle of Songs rests within the Thunderhead--a region in the northwest skies of Hyrule. Assuming that the other sky islands eventually returned to the surface along with Sky Keep, then the Isle of Songs would be in the prefect position to become the Forgotten Temple.

text:
Theory regarding Navi and the Downfall Timeline

I came up with a fan theory that creates one potential explanation for the creation of the downfall timeline along with how it ties into Navi's actions in the game Ocarina of Time. So the adult and child timeline are a direct result of Zelda sending Link back in time. But there is no actual reasoning for the downfall timeline. The lore given by Nintendo is simply “It's a timeline where the Hero of Time failed” but that's just a description, not an explanation for how the timeline was created within the context of the in game events.

Now consider for a moment how the Ocarina of Time works. When Zelda sends Link back in time, she is one playing the Ocarina. So the Ocarina doesn't actually travel back in time along with the traveler, thus creating separate timelines. In Majora's Mask, Link takes the Ocarina along with him everytime he rewinds time, theoretically preventing new timelines from forming. He's not going back and making a new reality, but erasing the events as a whole and starting over.

Now here's the theory part. Remember how when you first started the Ganondorf fight, Navi wasn't there to help you. She says something along the lines of “his evil aura prevents me from getting close to him” or something. And for the first portion of the fight you don't have Z-targeting. Then after the tower collapse sequence, Ganon rises from the ashes and you fight him again. However this time Navi declares “He won't hold me back this time! We will win this together!” and you get your Z-targeting back. What if, in the original timeline, Link fails because Navi wasn't able to help him. Without Navi's guiding light, Link dies in battle against Ganon in the final fight. Zelda makes a last ditch effort to send Navi back in time, to the exact moment the second fight starts. Because she is the key. So the creation of the downfall timeline is a result of Navi directly. That's why in the actual game, the moment the second phase starts, Navi is determined to not fail this time. Link wins, Ganon is sealed, and Hyrule is saved. But Navi alone knows what truly happened. That's why at the very end of the game, she leaves. She leaves knowing that she did not fully keep her promise to the Great Deku Tree to protect Link. Racked with guilt, she returns to the forest.

text:
[TotK] Totk's Fire Temple is just some of the least fun I've ever had playing Zelda.

I wanted to like it. On paper, a sprawling underground minecart network beneath Death Mountain sounds like a brilliant throwback to classic 3D Zelda dungeons, leaning into verticality and interconnected tracking. But the actual execution completely falls apart under the weight of the game's sandbox design.

Instead of navigating a tightly designed puzzle box where every room flows naturally into the next, you're tossed into a confusing, visually repetitive maze of grey stone tracks and identical-looking platforms. The cart navigation system is clunky, requiring you to constantly hit switches or build makeshift vehicles just to correct minor navigational mistakes. If you take a wrong turn or miss a stop, you aren't rewarded with a clever puzzle bypass—you're subjected to tedious backtracking or forced to awkwardly climb and Ascend through blank ceilings to brute-force your way past the intended layout.

Compare this to older fire-themed dungeons like Ocarina of Time's Fire Temple or Twilight Princess's Goron Mines, which gave you a clear sense of place, distinct architectural progression, and memorable music. TotK's Fire Temple feels less like a legendary ancient site and more like a half-assembled amusement park ride tossed down into the Depths.

[OoT] Lore behind the Skull Mask

The Skull Mask us one of eight masks you can wear in OoT. At first glance, it doesn't seem like much. Just a funny mask, nothing more.

However, if you talk to certain people, specifically, those in the woods, you can find some potential lore for the mask.

When talking to Saria, she'll say the mask reminds us of something she saw in the woods. At first, I thought she was talking about Skull Kid. But this is before we sell the mask to him. You Could say this is an oversight, but I think it's more likely meant to be a hint of who to sell the mask to.

Fado will compare you to a "Forest Ghost".

The most intresting one is the Deku scrubs in the Forest Stage. they reward you with more Deku Sticks, as the mask resembles their "sacred forest totem".

Theory

So, who or what is the skull mask based on? For Fado, it could just be a reference to the Stalfos, which she confirms to know about.

I noticed that the mask looks like a simplified version of the mask Phantom Ganon wore. Phantom Ganon being the boss of the Forest Temple.

Of course, it's unlikely Phantom Ganon is the figure Saria and the Deku Scrubs are talking about. However, it's possible that Ganondorf may have used a similar mask when requiting the Deku Scrubs to invade the Deku Tree.

The Deku appear to be your typical "false idol worshipers". This is shown in OoT when they regard Ghoma as their "queen", and later shown in FSA, when they worship Ganon, who, coincidentally, also places a Phantom of himself in the local Temple.

It's possible Ganondorf appeared to the Deku wearing the mask, claiming to be their god and appointing Ghoma as their queen. Saria, who spends a lot of time in the Lost Woods, may have seem a glimpse if this, but may not have thought of it. She may have just thought he was a regular forest spirit.

In the adult half, Ganondorf would create Phantom Ganon, based on himself as the "Forest Totem".

EDIT:

somebody suggested they might actually see the Stalfos as their "Forest Totem". Ganondorf may have still used a mask to trick the Deku into thinking he was their god.

[OOT] The Forest Temple and Forest Spirits

In OoT there are six temples for the six sages (unfortunately, we only get to explore five). Whilst four of them (light, fire, water and spirit) are unambiguously places of worship. The Shadow and Forest Temples are a bit more murky.

Of course, they are both be places of religious significances. But not specifically designated for "worship". The Shadow Temple seems to serve to keep wickedness locked up. Apparently by executing evil people within the Temple, so their evil spirits stay imprisoned. In contrast, the souls of the good usually move on to a better place, only lingering if they have unfinished business, like protecting personal treasure, as seen with Dampe and the Composer Brothers.

But what about the Forest Temple?

As many people have already worked out, the Forest Temple was not designed by the Kokiri, despite them being main inhabitants of the forest. The Temple doesn't even seem important to the Kokiri. Saria's the only one who visits the sacred forest grove, which she calls her "secret place".

Who these people were? We can't say for certain, but they appear to have been human.

What's interesting is that, when we meet Saria in the grove, she tells us she's going to teach us how to talk to the spirits in the forest. She then teaches us "Saria's song" which allows us to talk to her instead. This makes sense, as the Kokiri are spirits, although it still seems weird she would use this wording instead of just saying "I'll teach you a song that will let you talk to me". It's possible Saria was merely being facetious, although it could also be foreshadowing that her and Link are different species. That Link is not a spirit of the forest.

Saria would later talk about "Forest Spirits" in a different context, but I'll get to that later.

Given the context that the Deku Tree and the Kokiri are spirits, it's possible that Temple was built to honour them.

Although the Deku Tree is often seen as strictly being the guardian of the Kokiri/Koroks, he also appears to be an important figure for the Hylians. Often being tasked with guarding important artefacts, like the Master Sword (BotW) or even the Triforce (EoW).

I've already made a theory about the Koroks. But the basics are, the Deku Tree is a full grown Korok (as implied by TotK itself). Also, the Deku Tree did NOT change the koroks into Kokiri, but rather, produced the Kokiri as they appear in the game, in preparation for Link's arrival.

Spirits of the Lost Woods and Forest Temple

As I said before, Saria mentions "Forest Spirits" in a different context. This being, when she enters the Forest Temple due to said spirits calling out for help.

It's likely these "Forest Spirits" are actually the Poe Sisters, who were cursed by Ganondorf.

We also see other undead both in the Temple and Lost Woods as a whole. The Stalfos and the Skull Kids, who are lost non-fairy folk. Respectively adults and children who got lost in the woods and perished. Skull Kids, in particular, can be talked to by playing the Ocarina

In a bizarre twist. The original forest spirits (Koroks) become the forest people (Kokiri), meanwhile the forest people (humans) become the forest spirits (undead).

text:
A lot of players don't like breakable weapons because of loss aversion. There is a solution to this.

There's an issue that has plagued Breath of the Wild and Tears of the Kingdom: Loss Aversion. You explore the world and stumble upon a cool-looking weapon; some players will feel bad if they break that cool-looking weapon. By engaging in combat you lose your weapons - yes you can easily obtain more, but for many players it still doesn't feel good.

In Tears, you can even stumble upon entirely unique weapons. Breaking those extra-special weapons feels even worse - yes you can purchase replacements, but the game doesn't communicate this well and it's a pain to do regardless. Those unique weapons also aren't mechanically very interesting. They don't have unique moves, so some players will end up just displaying them in their house as trophies.

I propose a solution that addresses the issues with both Loss Aversion and Unique Weapon: Weapon Fragments and Weapon Memories.

Weapon Fragments are obtained automatically whenever you break a weapon. The stronger and more durable the weapon, the more fragments you get. And you can only obtain Fragments by breaking weapons. Now, by engaging in combat and smashing weapons, you always obtain something of value. Weapons will no longer just shatter when thrown at enemies, and throwing weapons into a pit will not yield Fragments. You must deplete a weapon's durability by attacking enemies or by smashing crates and ore and such. So what do you spend Fragments on?

Unique Weapons now have Weapon Memories, which are shown in the weapon tab of your inventory. By selecting a Memory, you can spend Weapon Fragments to transfigure a Common Weapon into a specific Unique Weapon. This has two purposes. One, each Unique Weapon you find can be viewed in your inventory at all times as a indication of permanent progress. Two, Unique Weapons are now available at all times - they still break, but all you need are a Common Weapon and enough Fragments to obtain one again.

With this system in place, players now have an active reason to use their weapons against enemies. You always get a special currency for breaking weapons, and that currency lets you use the extra special weapons. Those Unique Weapons, by the way? They cannot be dropped like normal weapons. Using the throw weapon button will instead activate an ability unique to each weapon. Each Unique Weapon you obtain unlocks a new combat move, their use of which is only limited by how many Fragments you have on hand.

Perhaps the devs will end up overhauling how weapons work. But personally, I think that breakable weapons are a good system that just needs some extra mechanics in place to address the issue of Loss Aversion.

Upgrading Link's puzzle-solving and traversal tools is more fun than upgrading hearts.

In Ocarina of Time, the Hookshot gets upgraded to the Longshot. In Skyward Sword, you can upgrade your Beetle to give it a speed boost. In Breath of the Wild, you can upgrade Stasis to make it usable directly against enemies, and upgrade Remote Bombs to make them deal more damage.

Here's some ideas for upgrade tiers to a Boomerang item as it could appear in an open-air Zelda game:

Gale Boomerang: Can now pick up objects like Bombs and Weapons, letting it deal damage to enemies based on what gets caught in the whirlwind.

Storm Boomerang: Targeted enemies will now get ragdolled when caught in the whirlwind, making it a very effective tool for stunning.

And here are some possible upgrades that past items and powers might have had:

Deku Leaf Upgrade - Link will swing the Leaf more quickly and the projectile will deal damage to enemies.

Spinner Upgrade - Can boost forward once along the ground to deal good damage to enemies.

Cryonis Upgrade - Ice Blocks will explode when shattered, damaging and freezing enemies nearby.

Ultrahand Upgrade - Held objects can be made to perpetually spin, making them deal more damage to enemies they collide with.

If the devs can implement a fairly large number of unique abilities, upgrading those abilities could be a really satisfying reward for exploration.

text:
[BotW][TotK] Shrines are a bad substitute for dungeons

Something I see a lot when the quantity/quality of dungeons in the Wild era games gets called into question is the idea that dungeons haven't really gone anywhere, they've just been broken down into shrines and sprinkled across the open world. I'm sure this was the Zelda team's intent, and on paper it's not a terrible idea... but I think the execution totally misses the mark.

Go back to Zelda 1 and try to break its dungeons down into individual "puzzles". You wind up with a very small pool of interactions: pushing a block, clearing a room of enemies, bombing a wall. Not great for a "puzzle game", but then the fun of dungeons didn't come from puzzle execution. It came from entering these mysterious cryptic spaces, riddling out where these interactions could happen, and using them as stepping stones in the larger navigation puzzle of exploring/mastering the dungeon. Along the way you'd deal with traps and enemies, find new tools and upgrades, and leave the dungeon feeling like you'd made major progress. Later Zelda dungeons would make the puzzle interactions more complex and cut down on navigation complexity, but I think this basic appeal stayed consistent.

Now, let's think about shrines. You're generally presented with a single type of interaction (which is spelled out to you via text when you enter), always in a Portal-esque austere sound stage. There is no mystery, there is no connection to the larger world or structure of the game, there is no reward or progress apart from a predictable fractional upgrade to your health/stamina. This is only puzzle execution, in a vacuum, at the expense of everything else.

If I throw out my expectations for Zelda games and try to appreciate the shrines as puzzles on their own terms... I still don't think most of them are very good. How could they be? The fact that they can be played in any order means you can't have the kind of difficulty curve or elaboration on mechanics that you see in puzzle games like Portal, Baba Is You, etc. The designers have an impossible task of making 120-150 "Level 1"s. It's not shocking that they pad out this number with Tests of Strengths and Rauru's Blessings.

Worth noting that I think the quests to find shrines can be really great! This is where all the fun stuff about Zelda puzzles lives in the Wild era games IMO: mystery, discovery, danger, connection to the larger world. The only bad part about these is that they all end with, y'know, the player finding another shrine.

text:
"Nintendo NEVER cared about Zelda's story"

"Nintendo NEVER cared about the story" is a common refrain in discussions about the Zelda series, and while I know I'm probably preaching to the converted here I wanted to write out some thoughts about it.

Here are a few quotes from a 2007 Wired interview with Yoshiaki Koizumi:

…my ambition had always been to make drama. That was my goal: Having a character, in a certain kind of world, having him go through a series of actions to accomplish something, and creating a dramatic tension throughout that. And games seemed like a really good opportunity to create a kind of drama that you don't find in films.

EAD doesn't tend to focus on the big story in most of their games. But I was the one coming up with scenarios, just on my own, ever since the time of Link's Awakening. But even at that time, I felt like I came up with this entire scenario and a backstory for Link, but nobody really seemed to care. They were always saying, let's not try to push the story forward too much.

So I would sort of try to find sneaky ways to get it in without them noticing too much. For example, I always liked the idea of you coming upon another character and hearing little bits of conversation that slowly begin to reveal different parts of the story. And that was the way that I tried to work on Ocarina of Time and Majora's Mask.

A brief summary of Koizumi's Zelda credits:
Wrote the manual and backstory for A Link to the Past
Designer/writer of Link's Awakening
Designer/director of Ocarina of Time and Majora's Mask (alongside Eiji Aonuma)
Assistant director of Wind Waker

Worth highlighting that many of the major plot elements Zelda fans like theorizing about (ex. the timeline split) come from these games. Also worth pointing out that some of the games that generate the most discussion about their themes/meaning/etc. (Link's Awakening, Majora's Mask) had heavy involvement from Koizumi.

My point here is not that Koizumi is the sole auteur responsible for Zelda having a story in spite of Nintendo. Koizumi IS Nintendo. Nintendo games are made by many different people with varying interests and priorities. I think it's likely that others who have played key roles in the development of Zelda games have had feelings about story closer to Koizumi's than Miyamoto's.

To be clear, you don't have to think any Zelda game's story is good. You don't have to care about the stories. You're free to speculate that a specific Zelda game was made by people who didn't care about its story. You can even be skeptical about whether the overarching continuity between Zelda stories is being cared for - that's a separate conversation.

What you can't do is tell people that nobody involved in making any Zelda game ever cared about story. You can't tell people they're delusional for noticing and caring about story in these games, or pretend that it's all fanfiction that Nintendo has been cowed into playing along with. You can't accuse people of being unreasonable for expecting or wanting story elements in Zelda games to reflect that the people who worked on them did, in fact, care.

All I can think of is the autumnal trees in Akkala (which seem to just be their regular colors) and the Frozen Hyrule stage in FSA (which may be unnatural? been awhile since I played it). Then of course there's Oracle of Seasons, but that game doesn't take place in Hyrule. Can anyone else think of anything? Edited to add: The fishing hole in TP! Totally forgot about it...

There's some evidence pointing away from Hyrule having regular seasons actually, like how when it becomes The Great Sea, the climate seems to be sub-tropical, with palm trees found across the whole map (Interestingly, Windfall Island has pine trees instead?)

There's also the presence of the Gerudo Desert to the west of Hyrule. Now obviously this is a magical fantasy world, but in real life most deserts form within a certain range of the equator, so Hyrule must be as well. And seasonal differences become less and less as you approach the equator, so...

I always wonder if anyone on the Zelda team has ever thought of these things, lol. Maybe not, but it is kind of surprising that Hyrule has existed as a fictional world for 40 years now and yet it's never been portrayed in fall or winter.

text:
I want Nintendo to take another crack at co-op Zelda, and the Switch is the perfect platform on which to do it.

It seems as though the existing multiplayer games failed to make much of an impression on people (I rarely see them brought up in online discussions), and I think I know why. The hardware configurations required by each game are a bit of a barrier to entry for most people. The handheld games (FS and TFH) required each player to have both their own handheld and their own copy of the game. If you're the only one in your friend group that has TFH, or the only one in your friend group that has a 3DS, tough luck. FSA required not only a GC and a copy of the game, but a GBA and a GC to GBA link cable for each player. I don't think I've ever seen a GC to GBA link cable in person.

A co-op Zelda game on the Switch wouldn't necessarily have that problem. A game designed for couch co-op could be played with one console and one copy of the game. Furthermore, the Switch comes bundled with two controllers (the Joy Cons); you wouldn't even need to buy additional controllers if you wanted to play with one other person. As far as hardware is concerned, the barrier to entry could be super low. The option to play over local wireless or the internet should still be there, of course.

A few years ago, Aonuma said he wanted to evolve the 2D formula. While co-op Zelda isn't a new idea, it would be functionally new for many people thanks to the inaccessibility of the older games. Furthermore, there's still a lot of space to explore with co-op Zelda. The team could experiment with asymmetric characters - rather than having both (or all) characters play as Link, maybe one character is Link and one character is Aryll. Maybe Aryll is smaller and so can't lift heavy objects, but her small size means she can fit into tighter spaces. The team could experiment with a more traditional, contiguous experience rather than chopping the game up into discrete, arcadey levels. Etc.

I think there's a lot of potential here. I'm sure co-op Zelda sounds appealing to a lot of people, but past attempts didn't sell that many copies (at least by the standards of the Zelda series) thanks in part to their hardware requirements. I think a co-op Zelda with a lower barrier of entry has the potential to reach a lot more people, and the Switch is the perfect platform for such a game.

text:
[OC] My idea for a new Zelda: Industrialized Hyrule, four playable heroes, and a very different Ganondorf

I've been thinking about what I'd like to see in a future mainline Zelda game, and I ended up developing a pretty extensive concept. I wanted to share it with other Zelda fans and see what people think!

My goal isn't to throw out what makes Zelda special, but to find ways to build on its history while giving the next game its own identity. BOTW reinvented exploration, and TOTK expanded on that with its physics-based abilities and creative problem-solving. I'd love to see the next game take similarly ambitious risks.

Here are some of the ideas I've been playing around with.

An industrialized Hyrule
I'd like to see Hyrule after a long period of peace, with technology and industry having developed considerably. Rather than beginning with a kingdom just starting to industrialize, this Hyrule would already have large cities, factories, railways, airships, and extensive infrastructure.

I'd still want it to feel unmistakably like Zelda. Ancient ruins, mysterious temples, hidden secrets, and natural landscapes would coexist with the newer technology. The different regions and peoples of Hyrule could be more interconnected through transportation and trade, creating a world that feels like it has genuinely evolved.

Technology wouldn't necessarily be good or evil in itself. Its effects on different communities, how it's used, and who benefits from it could all become part of the story.

2. Four playable characters
One of my biggest ideas is to have four playable heroes who can be switched between during solo play, with optional four-player co-op.

My initial lineup would be:

\- Link: The traditional swordsman and frontline fighter, specializing in swordplay, defense, and physical combat.

\- Zelda: A magical powerhouse who uses sacred abilities and her knowledge of Hyrule's history to manipulate magical energy and solve problems.

\- Linkle: An agile ranged fighter who uses dual crossbows, precision attacks, and mobility to control the battlefield.

\- Aryll: Link's sister from Wind Waker, reimagined as an adult inventor, engineer, and pilot. In an industrialized Hyrule, she'd have a natural place developing gadgets, manipulating machinery, and finding unconventional solutions.

I like the idea of bringing Linkle into a mainline game, and Aryll could be a particularly interesting choice because she would help establish the identity of this new Hyrule rather than simply bring back another familiar character.

The important part is that the four characters wouldn't just be interchangeable fighters with different weapons. Their abilities would change how you explore, solve puzzles, traverse the world, and approach combat.

For example, a puzzle might have several possible solutions depending on which character you use. Combining abilities could open up additional possibilities, and team attacks could let the characters build on one another's strengths.

I'm also a fan of the party synergy in Final Fantasy VII Rebirth, and I'd love to see something similar here. Link and Zelda might combine swordplay with sacred magic, while Linkle and Aryll could coordinate ranged attacks with mechanical gadgets.

Co-op would be an optional extension of the same system, not a requirement. The game should still be designed from the ground up to work as a single-player Zelda adventure. But if another player wants to jump in, they can select a party member to control

3. A different kind of Ganondorf
For the antagonist, I'd want a new incarnation of Ganondorf who retains the spirit and ambition of previous versions but operates in a very different world.

Rather than simply conquering Hyrule through military force, he could be a charismatic political leader or industrial magnate who has genuinely improved some people's lives. He'd have real supporters and understandable reasons for gaining influence, even as he gradually centralizes power and exploits the systems he's helped build.

His influence would be felt before the heroes fully understand what's happening. The party might initially encounter seemingly unrelated problems before discovering that they connect to something much larger.

I'd want to preserve the traditional Zelda payoff of confronting Ganondorf at the end, but make the journey toward that confrontation feel different from previous games.

4. Music that tells the story
The soundtrack is another area where I'd like the game to experiment.

I've been particularly impressed by how BOTW and TOTK use recognizable musical ideas while giving their worlds distinct identities. I'd want this game to build on that approach rather than simply add electric guitars and heavy drums to make everything sound industrial.

Ganondorf could have a theme that combines elements of his familiar musical identity with a new, mechanical sound. Early in the game, we might hear fragments of the melody woven into factory rhythms, political ceremonies, or other seemingly unrelated pieces of music.

If Ganondorf's identity remains hidden initially, those musical fragments wouldn't be immediately recognizable. As the heroes uncover more of his influence, the theme could gradually develop until his first major appearance brings the complete, unmistakable melody to the forefront.

I'd also love for the four playable characters to have their own musical identities. I'm a big fan of character themes in games like Bravely Default, especially when the music brings the party together during a climactic battle.

Imagine a final confrontation where Ganondorf initially dominates the soundtrack with his rigid, relentless theme, only for the heroes' individual musical motifs to emerge as they work together. Eventually, the motifs combine into a single arrangement without losing their individual identities.

It would be a musical way to express the idea that cooperation doesn't require everyone to become the same.

5. Familiar Zelda, reimagined
Ultimately, I wouldn't want this to lose the elements that make Zelda special: exploration, intricate dungeons, memorable items and abilities, secrets, distinctive bosses, and the feeling that there's always something fascinating just beyond the next horizon.

The industrial setting and four-character party should create new ways to experience those elements, not replace them.

That's the central idea behind the whole concept: each new Zelda should have a reason to exist beyond being the next installment, and its innovations should make us appreciate familiar elements in new ways.

These are ideas I've been developing rather than a fixed game design, and I'm sure there are plenty of details that would need to be worked out. There are more elements I could share if there's interest, including a potential sequel to this idea. I'd be interested to hear what other Zelda fans think!

text:
Is it possible that some monsters, such as the various types of Blins, are actually as intelligent as humans?

I'd always assumed that they were just generic, dumb mobs like the less intelligent varieties of goblin in various fantasy series, but I'm starting to question that interpretation the more I think about it.

In the very first TLoZ game, we can encounter non-hostile Moblins who speak completely normally and ask Link not to tell anyone about their secret spots.

In Oracles, King Moblin again speaks without any stereotypical monster speak. He sounds like a regular, if imperious, guy, rather than a beast trying to string together a sentence. IIRC, even his underlings talk normally when you walk in on the house King Moblin retreats to following his defeat, at least in Oracle of Seasons.

In The Minish Cap, we find a Moblin pretending to be a human. IIRC, it speaks in completely normal sentences.

In The Wind Waker to this sections, we have the whole Moe love letter quest. I haven't played this quest myself to know how intelligent Moe is, but it should also be noted that literacy is a great deal harder than basic language. It's entirely possible that, even if Moe has stilted writing, that wouldn't be reflected in his speech.

In Twilight Princess, we see King Bulblin command an army on his own and, again, speak normally without any stilted dialogue. Midna even expresses surprise that he was able to speak. And while we don't see the Bulblins speak in dialogue, their body language and comparatively advanced kit compared to the Bokoblins in the same game make them seem more like an organized fighting force.

In Spirit Tracks, the pirates, composed of Big Blins and Miniblins, have literal tanks. Sure, they're seemingly made of wood, but they also seem to move under their own power across the Forest Realm without issue. That's a level of tech I don't really recall seeing aside from the ancient Sheikah, the Zonai, and the pre-Skyward Sword Lanayru region. Theoretically, it seems like they could make cars if they wanted to.

In Tears of the Kingdom, we find Bokoblins and Moblins mining in the Depths. In fairness, they don't seem anywhere near as intelligent here. There's no dialogue for them, and manual labor easily seems like something Ganondorf could just command them to do without them knowing why or what it really means.

All this to ask: what are the odds that the Blins, as well as potentially other monsters like Lynels, are actually entirely capable of speech and advanced thought, but are also just usually uninterested in doing anything aside from attacking normal people like humans, Zora, Gorons, and Rito?

[All] Religions of Hyrule Part 1: Humans

This is a post about the religions of Hyrule. This is going to be multiple parts. I don't know how many yet.

The Three Goddesses
Bit of an introduction.
The three most important deities of Hyrule are the Three Golden Goddess. Din, Nayru and Farore.
These three are the creators of the Zelda universe. And, along with the Triforce, appear to be worshiped by every race in some shape or form. Although, different races may place different levels of enthesis on a certain Goddess.

Hylia, Hylians and the Shiekah
Other then the Golden Goddesses, the main deity of the Hylians is the unseen goddess, Hylia, in which the Hylians get their name.
In addition to the statues and springs, Hylia is also worshiped through her decendents, the Hyrulian Royal Family. The most famous members being the various Princesses Zelda, all named after the mortal reincarnation of Hylia. (I'm NOT saying "All Zeldas are Hylia". I'm only saying they are named after her). This was already a tradition as confirmed by King Rhoam. Although a Prince in AoL briefly made it "law". The Princessess Zelda also seem to be priestesses.
The Shiekah are a subset of Hylians, who guard the Royal Family. This tradition presumably coming from SS Impa being Hylia's servant.

Trees and Leviathans
Although the Deku Tree is known for being the guardian of the Kokiri/Koroks (who I'll get to in another part), he is an important figure in Hylian culture, something made more clear in later games. In BotW he guards the Master Sword, and in EoW he guards the Triforce.
I previously made a post on how the Forest Temple of OoT may have been built by humans to worship the spirits of the forest. Specifically, the Deku Tree.
The Maku Trees I may discuss in the future.
We also have Levias, the Guardian of Skyloft. A figure revered by the Hylians (at the time, simply called "humans") who would be offered against bowl of Pumpkin Soup.
Leviathans would loose relevance amongst Hylians in the future. Ignoring the Wind Fish, who's significance to Hyrule, if any, is unknown and the Ocean King, who is the god of is own world, most Leviathan worship would be practiced by the Zora.
A possible exception by be Jabun in the WW. Whilst not confirmed, is assumed to have been worshiped by Hylians on Greatfish Isle. This would make sense, due to the flood making sea travel more important.

Gerudo
Unlike other humans in Hyrule, the Gerudo don't worship Hylia (maybe except briefly in the past) or the Royal Family. Instead, the main focus of their religion is "Ancestor worship".
The Goddess of Sand is often assumed to be an aspect of Din, but other theories suggest it may be a personification of the Gerudo ancestor. It's possible this figure might represent the founding member of Hyrule's Gerudo settlement.
The Hylians once believed the Goddess of the Sand to be "evil", but only because they were still enemies with the Gerudo at the time.

Part 2 is here: [All] Religions of Hyrule Part 2: Zora and Rito

[All] Religions of Hyrule Part 2: Zora and Rito

This is part 2. Part on is here: [All] Religions of Hyrule Part 1: Humans : r/truezelda

The Zora

The Sea Zora and Hylians have always been close allies. The River Zora, not so much. For know, lets mainly focus on the Sea Zora.

Of all the races in Hyrule, the Zora seem to be the ones that revere the most gods. Much like many races in Hyrule, the Zora believe in the three Golden Goddesses. The most important for them being Nayru. but they also have Lord Jabu-Jabu and are implied to worship Water Dragons.

Whereas the humans have their unseen deities, the Zora have a physical god, who protects them from the lake. That being Lord Jabu-Jabu.

The origins of Lord Jabu-Jabu are unknown, but he could be a decendents of the Skyloft Guardian Levias. If this is true, it may shed some light on how he became the patron Deity of the Zora.

Years ago, I came up with a theory that the Zora are some kind of Dragonborn equivalent. That being Tadtones, Parella, and the Water Dragon Faron are all the same species, but in different stages or castes. And they eventually evolved into the Zora. Note: whilst it's too late to reply on the linked post, you can still share your thoughts on that theory here.

If the Zora are descended from the Water Dragon, this would explain their worship of Levias' presumed decendents. Levias was leader of the three dragons, after all. On top of that, it would also explain the water dragon imagery within the Water Temple.

Speaking of water dragons, the Light Spirt Lanayru, who resides in Lake Hylia, resembles a dragon. It is also the only Light spirt that has a shrine. further showing how the Zora take deity worship very seriously.

The Zora of Termina are no different. Whilst everyone in Termina presumably worship the four giants, the Zora also have the Giant Turtle. This Turtle in similar to the Giants in which it, like them, watches over it's area in it's sleep, and can be summoned with a song. As far as I can tell, the Giant Turtle is the only god we see that isn't one of the Four Giants.

The Rito

In WW, the Rito are evolved from the Zora. Much like their aquatic ancestors, their culture also revolves around a physical god: the Sky Spirit Valoo. The also have shrines dedicated to the wind gods: Zephos and Cyclos.

These Rito are extremely co-dependent on their god. They must obtain a scale from the dragon, or they wont be able to grow wings.

text:
Where does Ocarina of Time truly rank all time as of the year 2026?

I'm 37 years old, and growing up, Ocarina of Time (OOT) was by far the coolest/greatest video game I'd ever played. That includes games I played later, like Call of Duty in college on PS3. Don't get me wrong—online COD is incredible, but the overall storyline and world of OOT are still unmatched in my opinion. I'm not a hardcore gamer, so I never played Breath of the Wild or many of the other games that consistently rank near the top of the "greatest games of all time" lists. I did play Red Dead Redemption 2, which is also frequently ranked very highly. RDR2 was a great game, and obviously its graphics and physics are on another level compared with OOT. But that's not really what I'm talking about when I compare the two. I'm talking about the overall game—the story, world-building, progression, interconnectedness, etc. Obviously, modern graphics and physics can enhance a game tremendously, but I don't think they automatically make a game better. For example, no matter how brilliant the writing is, I don't think a 2D Zelda game could ever have the same overall impact as a 3D Zelda game. But conversely, if the storyline and world-building of a game are inferior to OOT, I don't think better graphics and physics can make up the difference. That's basically how I felt playing RDR2. It was an incredible game, but in my mind, it didn't come close to OOT. Over the past week or so, I watched a ~10-hour video of someone playing through OOT on YouTube. I honestly wondered if maybe I was just looking back at it through the eyes of a kid and remembering it as being better than it actually was. But man...no. It really was that amazing. You have the eight main dungeons, but there's SO much happening in between. There are essentially "mini-levels." You have to actually discover and figure out how to access the temples. The Ocarina itself is woven into the entire game. The way everything connects and builds on what came before is just incredible. So that's the question I'm hoping gaming enthusiasts can answer: Are there any games released since OOT that are truly on the same level of greatness? I'm not trying to be a homer for my childhood or my generation. If there's a game that surpasses OOT, then it is what it is. I'm genuinely curious whether there are games out there that I haven't played that can give me that same feeling. I'd really like an objective perspective from people who have played a lot more games than I have. What games, if any, do you think are genuinely in the same tier as Ocarina of Time?

Who is working on the OoT Remake, and what would it imply?

With the news about the OoT remake dropping last month and most people being fairly confident in it, one thing that is really making me curious is, who exactly is working on it? Given the main Zelda team finished TotK in 2023 and there was no DLC planned, I think most people expected that the next game they were working on would be the next Zelda game. I am sure that regardless of what happens that is still true and the next "Switch 2 Only" Zelda game is certainly being worked on right now. However with the OoT remake apparently being developed, it does leave me curious as to whether the main zelda team is primarily working on it instead. OoT is imporant, no one doubts that so I do think that we could see an actual Zelda team working on it. If they are, I wonder if its being worked on by the majority or a large portion of the team that worked on ToTK is working on this remake. Personally, that would actually make me upset, since I really do want to see an actual new Zelda game. But as much as it pains me I could see Nintendo feeling that a OoT remake needs that especially hands on approach and would count as a true "main" game, especially depending on the scope like if its fully a Final Fantasy 7 style remake. Heck, given we know the last year or so of TotK's dev cycle was pure polish, given how not every dev by far would actually be helpful for just polishing things I could see those types working on the next project, just while previously I thought that next project would be the next Zelda game instead its potentially this OoT Remake. Alternatively, I could see it just being worked on by a splinter of the main Zelda team, perhaps in conjunction with some third party devs(Grezzo?). Admittedly, most game studios are big, and while I don't know the specifics at all its not at all uncommon for multiple projects to be worked on in conjunction(heck, I'd say its rarer if a studio really is working on just one thing; thats a recipe for disaster). Though there is usually one project that is "prioritized". And of course the other main option would be its more like Echoes of Wisdom where its developed by another closely aligned studio but just with some executive oversight from Aonuma. To summarize, basically do you think this game is made directly by the Zelda team or a third party, and do you think OoT remake is "the next big Zelda game" and so the next actually "new" Zelda game could potentially be further off than some people hoped.

text:
Bite-sized Zelda games

A good while back I floated the idea that Nintendo could continue serving us new 2D Zelda games through a theoretical Zelda Maker. Zelda Maker could come with a small Zelda game built using the included assets and made by the Nintendo team. Whenever they released DLC with new assets and features to be used in the Maker, a new, bite-sized Zelda would be released alongside it. Instead of ~$60 for a new full fat 2D Zelda every few years (or, as of late, never) it would be ~$20 every year or two for a small Zelda game, packaged with the new maker assets. What kind of games would you want to see if we started getting more frequent bite-sized releases instead of infrequent larger games? Would you want each of these games to be a totally standalone adventure with a new Link? Should the games all be part of a single, continuous series following the story of one Link? Or would you rather each game continue the story of another hero we've already met? Personally, I think it could be really interesting to have an 'epilogue' for games we've played like Twilight Princess or Skyward Sword, where we get to see what happens to those characters next. It would mesh well with the concept of releasing a new set of unique assets with each game, matching the art style of the source game. On the other hand, establishing brand new stories can be better than living in the past. And it's always possible to retroactively spoil a satisfying story by tacking more onto it.
